title: The Bench · The Deposit
subtitle: A different night, a different pair — the town that emptied, and the deposit that keeps running away.

customObject.name: a park bench
customObject.description: the same worn wooden bench under the lamps — someone has carved something small on the back rail

script.note: The night garden again. A weeknight this time. An older man and a younger one — neighbours of the sort who only ever talk at the bus stop, finally sitting down.

script.text: You don't have to keep me company, Tomas. I'm just doing my maths. I do it out here so I don't do it at the kitchen table in front of my wife.
Deposit maths?
Deposit maths.
How far off?

Three years. Which is what I said three years ago. It's the only number I know that doesn't go down when you pay it. We save, the prices climb, the goalposts jog away at exactly our speed. It's beautifully calibrated. Like it was designed.
Mm. I owned a house once. Whole house. You'd have hated the town, though — everyone said it was nowhere. Mill town. When the mill went, the work went, and the town emptied out like a bath.
That's where you're from? You never said.

Nobody asks an old man where he's from, they ask him to keep the noise down. — Here's the thing though. That nowhere town. When my roof came off in the storm of ninety-one, I had eleven men on it by Saturday. I didn't hire them. I knew them. I'd been on their roofs.
Eleven. I've got four hundred contacts in this phone and I couldn't raise two of them for a roof.
And I've got no mill and no town. So between us we make one whole life, eh?

That's the trade nobody names. You move to where the work is, and the work is real — but everyone around you is a stranger with headphones in. My street is full at night and empty in every way that counts. I know the delivery times of my neighbours better than their names.
In the mill town, work was scarce and people weren't. Here, people are scarce and work isn't. Some clerk somewhere decided those were the only two products on the shelf.
So which do you pick?
You don't pick. That's my point, lad. Picking between work and people is like picking between food and water. A place that makes you choose is a badly built place.

My cousin and I ran the numbers once — joke numbers, beer numbers. If four households pooled deposits, we clear a whole building in the cheap end of town in under two years. Everyone said the same thing: 'never buy with people'. Then everyone went home alone to keep renting from a stranger who owns forty doors.
'Never buy with people.' We used to RAISE BARNS with people. Half the world got built by four families and a shared ladder, and one bad century talked us all out of it.
You'd need the right people. That's the whole game, isn't it. Not the deposit. The people. Choosing them — instead of getting whoever the rent gods send.

script.note: Tomas turns, slowly, and squints at the back rail of the bench — at a small carving, recent, the varnish still pale in the cut.

script.text: Heh. Look at that. Someone's carved on the rail here. 'M and D — people first.' Vandalism, technically.
…Whoever they are, they had this exact conversation on this exact bench. That's either a coincidence or a queue.

Then put our initials down for the queue. Bring the beer numbers on Sunday — the real ones, not the joke ones. I've got forty years of knowing how a town dies. Be useful to help build one that doesn't.
Sunday. And Tomas — ask me where I'm from, sometime. Nobody's asked me either.
Sunday, then. Two questions on the agenda.

script.note: The lamps hum. Two more initials join the rail before they leave — scratched shallow, easy to deny, impossible to unsee.
